title: I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere) - YouTube
content:
I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere) - YouTube

Genius piece of OSINT by Colsto, who demonstrates how you can take almost imperceptible background noise of planes from a video soundtrack, figure out their Doppler curves, then cross reference them against ADS-B data to find the exact location of the video based on their speed, distance, and gaps between different flights.

Via Lobste.rs

title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
content:
A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.

The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network1 was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement.

I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks. Figuring out what game a model was trained to play based on the network sounds impressive until you consider three points:

  1. The input channels of the model directly listen to each 8x8 grid cell
  2. The input channels are labeled (e.g. “agent”, “moving objects”)
  3. It’s thus relatively trivial to calculate2 which parts of the grid the first layer of weights cares about and why

Here’s that calculation expressed as a heatmap in three lines of Python:

d = np.load("a9f535cc.npz")
W1 = d["actor/dense1/kernel"]
norms = np.linalg.norm(W1.reshape(10,10,5,32).transpose(2,0,1,3), axis=-1)  # 5 x 10 x 10

And here’s the heatmap for each game:

If someone showed you that heatmap without the game labels, I think you’d be able to immediately identify at least the first three games purely by noticing where the player is (e.g. for Breakout, in a horizontal line at the bottom) and where the moving objects are (e.g. for Pac-Man, in the distinctive Pac-Man maze). It’s neat3 that Astra was able to calculate the norms in its head without executing Python, but not that impressive, and certainly not something that should shock anyone who’s been paying attention.

I’m not going to go through each example4 in the paper, so let’s skip straight to the most impressive one: fixing a 0.8B Qwen model’s ability to do mathematics. 0.8B is a lot of parameters, and “mathematics” is way more complicated than “guess what the game is based on how the player moves”, and editing weights is arguably harder than parsing them. What happened here?

First, note that the Qwen model was not “bad at mathematics” in a pure capabilities sense. It had a specific problem where after 32k tokens it would get stuck in loops, so any mathematical task that needed more than 32k tokens would automatically fail5. If you had a model that looped like this, how would you update the weights to fix it? Personally, I would try steering: I would write some reasoning texts that looped and some reasoning texts that didn’t, calculate the difference between the looping and non-looping residuals, measure how much each weight contributed to that difference, then try manually trimming those top weights. This is basically the Heretic abliteration playbook.

And this is exactly what Astra did! It wrote four pairs of texts, measured6 the weights that contributed to looping, started cutting them down and testing if it worked, and ended up finding a patch that stopped the Qwen model from looping, thus making it able to work on mathematical problems for more than 32k tokens. Again, this is exactly what a competent human researcher could have and would have done.

It’s cool that Astra was able to make direct weight updates. But we shouldn’t think of this like a radically new capability that will change how AI research is done. We should think of this as analogous to the ability of LLMs to emit machine code and tweak compiled binaries: it’s an impressive trick, but the best way to work with binaries is still to write source code and compile it. Likewise, the best way to update the weights of a model is to train it normally. To the extent that intelligent LLMs help with AI research, they will help by improving training, not by magically tweaking model weights directly.

  2. By taking the L2 norm of each input across the 32 weights in the first layer.

    ↩

  3. Note that this is superhuman mental mathematics, not superhuman AI research.

    ↩

  4. The most impressive one I’m skipping is hand-writing a neural network from scratch. While cool, if you can express a task as a simple program, we already know it’s possible to express that program as a NN, even by unaugmented humans.

    ↩

  5. All the <32k token problems were solved successfully on the original Qwen model.

    ↩

  6. Unlike with the toy game networks, it had access to Python.

title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
content:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linux Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

title: Apple Announces Record $114.5B Fourth-Quarter Results
content:
Jason Snell, Six Colors:

On Monday, Apple announced record fourth-quarter earnings, with total revenue of $114.5B, up 12 percent from the year-ago quarter. iPhone revenue was up 17.5%, Mac revenue was up 23.7%, and Services revenue was up 9.8%. Wearables revenue was down 7.9% and iPad revenue was down 10.4%. [...]

And now, to help you visualize what Apple just announced, here is our traditional barrage of charts and graphs.

As usual, Snell also has a transcript of the analyst call — Ternus’s first as CEO. My favorite tidbit was his line at the end of this answer:

Richard Kramer, Arete Research: Your latest MacBook Pros included more iOS features like Touch and Dynamic Island as well as, obviously, Siri AI. Should we anticipate further close linking of macOS and iOS features, maybe even pointing at some point to a single unified OS, either for simplicity or to reduce costs?

John Ternus: Look, we are very proud of both the Mac and the iPad, and I think what you’ve seen over the years is we’ve really enjoyed the ability to bring features and capabilities across the ecosystem and create really compelling features that span things between handoff between iPhone and Mac and iPad, and so when we design the product, we’re looking at how can we make the best version of each and every product, and if you look at what we just did last week with the MacBook Pro, we took a huge leap forward. These MacBook Pros are better in every way than the ones that came before them, and we’re really proud of that, and so we don’t have any fundamentally different changes that we’re planning right now, nor would we talk about it anyway.

 ★

title: Prove you are not a child
content:
I'm 100% for banning social media for children. I would even extend it to banning it all together in its current form. But I am also against the methods for enforcement.

The problem with banning social media for one group and not another is that you have to differentiate the different groups somehow. And right now, in an age where information and personal data means everything, there are several entities that are salivating to get this data.

I've written before about all the problems that come from uploading sensitive data online. It doesn't even matter if they delete the data afterward, as long as the data goes through the wire in the first place, there is a chance for a leak.

What appears to be the same simple request "please verify your identity", becomes fundamentally different when mediated by technology. The question isn't whether these digital systems will be compromised, but when. And unlike that movie theater clerk who can't perfectly recall my birthdate minutes after seeing it, computers have perfect memory. They store, copy, backup, and transmit our most sensitive information through networks we don't control, to companies we've never heard of, under policies we'll never read.

When kids are not allowed to use social media, it's the adult who pays the price. It's the adult who has to prove that they are not children. They have to risk uploading their government ID to a third party, or biometric data that may be saved and backed up forever.

I reject this method.

I also reject the method where I have to provide my age to the operating system. No system should compel me to provide personal data in order to use it. Especially if this feature is intended to provide the information to a third party. And what happens if I don't provide this information to my freebsd machine? Or worse, what if I provide false information? Am I going to get punished? How does that protect children in any way?

Breaking news: Grown up arrested when OS reported forged identity in his laptop.

One question I asked myself was what happens when a minor circumvents the ban. What are the consequences? At least in Australia, a country that has implemented a social media ban for those under 16, there are no consequences.

The law places legal responsibility on platforms, not children or parents, and it currently applies to Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.

This almost sounds reasonable. Why should you care, if it becomes facebook responsibility when you don't even own a facebook account? But there is always a caveat. When facebook becomes a tool your school uses to communicate with parents. When Google classroom is the service students use to do their homework. When you are required to login on a system to receive government service. You may not care about a particular social media, but they raise the bar for every other entrant in the game. Every website frequented by a large number of people inherently become social media, and demand data you didn't need to provide before.

Technology is not a magical thing that can just solve every problem. It is especially weak when it comes to social problems. However, society can use technology to solve their problems. The responsibility of children falls onto their parents. And there are great tools for parents that their kids access on their devices.

title: Pumpkin Seeds
content:
Some spare ephemera about Halloween, at exactly the time you need it: A couple days after the fact. We got cryptids, celebs, and even an original tune.

Hey all, Ernie here with a piece from David Buck! He’s here to talk about the most tedious holiday, depending on how you hold it: Halloween. (It’s so tedious that we wrote about it late.)

Today in Tedium: Hey, everyone! I’m back! Anyhow, my love of Halloween isn’t dead, but it sure does smell funny these days. Over the past few years, we’ve published a few Halloween specials featuring plenty of spooky, Halloween-themed stuff. We even tried out a short video/podcast thingy. Last year, we presented a sequel of sorts. And this year, we’re continuing that tradition with some more Halloween-flavored treats for the spooky season. So grab yourself a Butterfinger, put on your favorite spooky tunes, and get ready for another helping of Pumpkin Spice Pop Culture. — David @ Tedium

Today’s GIF comes from a piece of classic cheese involving the late Tim Curry, one of the best to ever do it. More about that below.

1966

The year reports of a flying, humanoid monster being seen around Point Pleasant, WV. Sightings continued until late 1967. It was probably just migrating birds, but Mothman continued to be part of the public imagination. It’s perhaps just as recognizable as the Jersey Devil, Bigfoot, or Chupacabra in the Great Hall of Cryptids (an imaginary place I just made up, but, hey, it’d be a pretty bitchin’ museum).

Cryptids are the cream of the Halloween crop

Halloween isn’t complete without monsters. I’ve read about them, played TTRPG’s that feature them, and even drawn a few, like that mushroom bit baba yaga-style house above.

A few years ago, I was an avid viewer of Dr. Emily Zarka’s Monstrum. It’s a show about the monsters of cultures all around the world. She’s covered by the headless horseman (so have we!), King Kong, and cryptids from around the world.

Monsters are always a fascinating topic, particularly lycanthropes. But we got to thinking more about local cryptids. That is, cryptids specific to a certain area. You know, like the Jersey Devil. Only they’re not limited to the United States. These cryptids and stories about them have traveled across the world.

Cryptids have long been a fascinating subject for us, so we did a little roundup of the four of the most interesting local cryptids we came across.

My criteria for these was a) I think they’re interesting and b) I can draw them. You’ll see why that’s important in a moment.

If your favorite cryptid isn’t here, I apologize. They’re all great. These just happen to be the ones I like the most right now.

Grafton Monster: Grafton, WV. Ah, West Virginia, home to the original sightings of Mothman. The state has another cryptid in its history: the Grafton Monster. It’s supposed to be a tall and pale humanoid creature that may or may not be headless. Oh, and it makes a creepy (sometimes described as “unusual” whistle sound.

Just like our good buddy Mothman up there, sightings of the Grafton Monster began around 1964. Journalist Robert Cockrell described the monster as roughly 7 to 9 feet tall. He also said it looked kind of like a seal but it had no head. I imagine it looks a little something like my drawing above (it’s not to scale).

Dover Demon: Dover, MA. The east coast seems to be awash in cryptids. Massachusetts has the Dover Demon. This one is pretty odd. In 1977, a creature with glowing orange eyes that was only four feet tall was spotted on a broken stone wall. 17-year old Bill Bartlett drew a sketch

Over the next few nights, more sightings were reported. What the kids described sounded like a gray alien right out of Area 51.

What they might have actually seen was a baby moose or a snow owl. Either way, it’s a bizarre local cryptid story and has become legendary around that area of Massachusetts.

Tommyknocker: Georgetown, Colorado. Did you know that Tommyknockers are a real Colorado cryptid? No, these aren’t Stephen King’s Tommyknockers. Instead, these guys are like Colorado leprechauns.

They knock on things from inside a mine. You can’t see them, but they’re there, warning of impending cave-ins or helping miners out.

Sometimes, they’re friendly or described as tricksters. But they’re a Colorado legend, right along with the Yeti’s in Vail, those pesky vampires in Lafayette, and that silly little hotel that inspired The Shining in Estes Park.

Bunyip: Australia. The U.S. has its fair share of local cryptids, but you should see some of the ones from around the world. Take the bunyip, for example. This thing is scary. It’s from aboriginal culture, originally, and is said to resemble a hippo. Or a manatee. Or something with an elongated neck.

Either way, it’s an incredibly deadly creature lurking in a swamp in the inner part of the continent. According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, its origin might be related to the rare appearances of seals upstream in Australia. I suppose that makes sense, but imagine running into one of these things in the wild.

Cryptids often seem to be based on things that really do exist, but the way we imagine or interact with them is what creates the idea of a monster. The human imagination really is a powerful thing, isn’t it?

2012

The year I wrote a silly song for Halloween. Back in those days, I wrote silly bluesy folk songs. I still do. But I used to do it a lot more often. And I had a ton of fun songs. I’ve never managed to get enough energy together to make a full record. Life has been hectic. Lately, I’ve decided I want to return to what I liked most about this industry: playing music and writing about oddball stuff. With that in mind, I wanted to share the journey of a Halloween-adjacent song I wrote over a decade ago and never got around to until now. So I dug this song up from its grave.

A brand-new, oddball song for Halloween that never got the chance to live

Last year, we talked about Phish’s famous Halloween shows and a lot of other Halloween-themed music from some of our favorite musicians. This year, my costume is “nerdy guy who’s really into jam bands.” When you look at me, you can just tell I like Blues Traveler. A lot. (Editor’s note: I also enjoy Blues Traveler … when John Popper is not blocking me on social media.) So, of course, I’ll be talking more about my own foray into “scary melodies”.

I’ve been reflecting on something related to my personal musical journey. About a decade ago (perhaps a few years earlier), I wrote what I considered a “Halloween song.” My goal was to make a video for it, release it online, and submit it to The Dr. Demento Show.

As I’ve written previously, getting airplay on Dr. Demento was a singular dream of mine for a long time. It did eventually happen, but not until a few years before Dr. D announced his retirement. It’s been a year since the show ended.

So where does that leave my career ambitions? I dunno. I’ve been honing my craft and playing for fun for years. So it doesn’t really affect things much. The weird music pipeline is just a bit different.

But I want to talk about that Halloween song I wrote so many years ago. I called it “Beware, the Poltergeist” because I thought it sounded fun and kind of cool. It might have been based on a short story or TV episode, but I just don’t exactly recall where it came from.

I started the song, wrote some music, and finished a verse/pre-chorus, but have just never been able to finish or expand it meaningfully. It’s a bluesy tune about a poltergeist who’s kind of a jerk. I thought it was hilarious, and I dig the way I have the melody match the lyric.

The song starts like this (it was originally in the key of B):

There’s a ghost in my house
Trying to push me down a staircase
There’s a ghost in my house
Throwing things all over the place

See? This is just proof that you don’t need an LLM to write a dumb song. I was writing dumb songs years before ChatGPT hit the scene. Also, don’t use an LLM to help you be creative. If you didn’t bother to write it yourself, I don’t want to read or listen to it. Hey, look! Some clouds. I’ll be right back.

(Incomprehensible ranting and light swearing about outsourcing thinking and creativity in the direction of no one in particular)

Okay. I’m back. Anyhow, I wrote a chorus/pre-chorus. It isn’t Vonnegut, but I like it. I’m not sure if I actually want it to say much. After that, the song repeats the “there’s a ghost in my house” bit, followed by an off-hand comment about how much he sucks.

Obviously, the song isn’t going to make it onto the show now. But that’s not the reason I revisit it every so often. I like it. It’s fun to play. I just never managed to finish it. The other day, however, I realized something: it actually is finished, and it always has been. I was just overthinking it and playing it in the wrong tuning.

Not everything needs to be edited or rewritten to death. Sometimes, there’s value in a simple song with an extended guitar bit.

I never recorded it. Until now. So, this Halloween, I present the second-ever released song by my one-man band (which I’m calling Asthmatic Whales nowadays; it used to be The Nostalgia Ward): “Beware, the Poltergeist.”

And there you have it. A silly Halloween song for the truly scary times we’re living in. I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did dusting it off and revisiting it. Thanks for reading, and I hope you have a very Happy Halloween.

Those homebrew NES games Spirit Halloween sells? Surprisingly good

In last year’s NES roundup, I briefly mentioned how Spirit Halloween was selling NES carts containing the homebrew title Haunted: Halloween ‘86: The Curse of Possum Hollow. What I didn’t talk about is just how freaking amazing this game series is.
That’s one of three games in the series, alongside Haunted: Halloween ‘85, and Haunted: Halloween‘87: Year of the Witch.

You can pick the games up on Steam or Itch.Io, from the folks who made it, Retrotainment Games LLC. All their stuff is great. There are also physical cartridges on their official website, if you’re into that sort of thing.

These games are standouts among NES homebrew titles; they have a Double Dragon and Mighty Final Fight feel to them. However, the stories are more developed, you can switch characters, there are extra move sets (which is not typical in most NES games), and I had a ton of fun playing through them.

So let’s look at the trilogy. I only own the first two games (purchased directly from Itch.Io)

I haven’t had the opportunity to play Haunted: Halloween ‘87 yet, but if it’s anything like the first two (and particularly, like ‘86), I know I’m going to love it.

I think the first two are definitely standout titles and I recommend them for some 8-bit Halloween fun.

As far as NES Homebrew goes, I’m still pretty enthusiastic about it, all these years later.

33

The number of times I’ve mentioned or outright talked about The Dr. Demento show on Tedium. Although he’s been officially retired for a year now, I still listen to and collect the show. I haven’t been able to keep up with the community much (although I’d like to) due to life, but I know the fans are still out there. Halloween is a time we “Dementians” loved, so I always think about the show a lot more often around this time of year. I also couldn’t help but think that the good Doctor would have done a nice tribute to the late Tim Curry on his show back in August, if it hadn’t gone off the air.

This year has been a rough one, both for the world and in terms of some of our favorite entertainers passing.

We lost Tim Curry, Dolly Parton, and Patrick Stewart all within a few months of each other. In honor of these icons, here are a few fun facts about each that relate to Halloween:

  1. Tim Curry once recorded a classic cheeseball song for the low-budget ’80s HBO movie The Worst Witch called “Halloween Song.” As Gizmodo wrote about it in 2020, “It has remained one of the most wonderful, terrible, bizarre videos of all time, thanks to its unapologetic synthesizer score, baffling lyrics, and the cheapest special effects the ‘80s had to offer—but there’s more to it than its cheesiness. Much more.” (Speaking of Curry, check out this Rocky Horror Picture Show audience participation recording from 1983.)
  2. Dolly Parton was a Halloween enthusiast, and shared half a dozen separate costumes on her Instagram page last year. In the wake of her passing, her fans made her one of the most popular costume options this year.
  3. Patrick Stewart reportedly bought a haunted house in Hollywood, then rented it to someone without telling his tenants about it. (They figured it out, and then he came clean.) It’s a tale that he wrote about in his book Making It So: A Memoir.

It’s a sad time, but hopefully, we’ve been able to cheer you up and boost your spirits a bit during this Halloween season (which seems to be shrinking each year, or maybe I’m just getting old). Thanks for reading, and until next time, have a very Happy Halloween!

–

Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal! And thanks again David Buck for making this issue great as always.
